intro_en:
After the Small Crater (Makhtesh Katan) and the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol), the Israel National Trail advances towards the largest crater of all – Makhtesh Ramon – which we will reach in a few more segments.
Along the way we pass through landscapes different from those of the craters, and cross the Zin Valley (Bik'at Zin) and Nahal Zin. The beginning of the current segment is accompanied to the north by the flatirons of the Hatira Ridge. Further on, new scenery appears, with the "Zinim Cliff" (Matzok HaTzinim), which lies on the edge of the Avdat Plateau above the Zin Valley.

 Oron – Nahal Ofran (39)
 Hod Akev – Nahal Havarim (41)
transport_en: A bus runs to Midreshet Sde Boker.
important_en: Access to the starting point at the overnight campsite at the foot of Hod Akev is by 4x4 vehicle only.
It is very important to arrange water caching (and preferably food as well) at the end point at the Nahal Mador overnight campsite.
description_en:
We leave the overnight campsite in Nahal Mador onto a black-marked dirt road that passes close to the campsite. We advance with the road to the left, heading south-west, along the channel of Nahal Mador.
Before the road and the stream curve south to meet Nahal Zin, the trail turns right, leaves the road and enters a small channel between pale hills (the turn comes before the power line visible ahead of us).
We cross hills and channels. One of the channels we cross is called "Talul" (Steep), and the name suits it. Like Nahal Ofran, which we descended in the previous segment, it drops very steeply from the Hatira Ridge, between the flatirons that make up the south-eastern flank of the ridge – the Hatira anticline.
Our direction of walking, northwards, brings us closer to the ridge and the flatirons – seemingly the opposite of the Israel National Trail's general direction, south. The trail's route forms a loop, in order to place the overnight campsite close to a main dirt road, allowing convenient vehicle access to the campsite while at the same time reducing the damage to the environment and to nature caused by vehicles driving off-road.
We continue walking and stay alert so as not to miss the turn to the left. The turn is in an area of hamada – a surface covered in dark stones. A black-marked trail arrives from the right and joins the Israel National Trail at the point of the left turn.
After the turn, far off on the horizon ahead of us, stands the long ridge line of the Zinim Cliff, beyond the Zin Valley. We may already be able to make out Hod Akev – a conical peak on the right-hand side of the ridge, marking the direction and destination of our walk.
Along the way, the black marking accompanying the Israel National Trail marking changes to red and then back to black. We continue in the same direction until we cross the large, central channel of Nahal Zin, on a stretch marked red.
Nahal Zin is one of the largest streams in the Negev. Its source is in the Mitzpe Ramon area, on the rim of Makhtesh Ramon, and it flows into the Dead Sea. Its length from source to outlet is about 120 km.
At the start of its course, from the Mitzpe Ramon area to the Avdat Canyon (Ein Avdat), its flow direction is south to north. On leaving the Avdat Canyon it turns east towards the Arava. The sharp change in the stream's flow direction points to an ancient process of "stream capture": Nahal Zin, which cut back (westwards) as the Syrian-African Rift subsided, connected to channels that drained north towards Nahal HaBesor and the Mediterranean, and "captured" them – diverting their drainage to itself.
A short way after crossing Nahal Zin, we meet a black-marked trail arriving from the north, from Nahal Daroch. Together with the black marking we advance to the overnight campsite at the foot of Hod Akev in the Zin Valley.
Those who wish can walk a further 5 km or so, partly uphill, to Midreshet Sde Boker, where there are lodging options.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI)
